value.overview: The Turquoise Cotinga, also called Ridgway’s Cotinga, is a scarce forest bird restricted to the Pacific slope of Costa Rica and western Panama. The male is brilliant turquoise blue with dark wings and tail, while the female is predominantly brown and mottled. It usually remains high in the canopy, where it can be difficult to detect. The species depends on humid forest and is considered vulnerable because its limited habitat continues to be lost and fragmented.
value.classification: The Turquoise Cotinga is Cotinga ridgwayi in the family Cotingidae and order Passeriformes. It is a monotypic species and is closely related to several other blue cotingas.
value.identification: Adult males are striking turquoise or blue-green overall, with a dark eye area, blackish wings and tail, and darker flight feathers edged in blue-green. Females are much duller, mainly brown above and buff below, with pale or whitish spotting on the head and neck and darker markings on the underparts. Juveniles resemble females but commonly show buff or cinnamon edging on the wing feathers. Both sexes have a short, broad bill and dark gray legs.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from the southern Gulf of Nicoya and other Pacific lowlands of Costa Rica southward through the Osa Peninsula and nearby Pacific foothills into western Panama. In Costa Rica it is a resident of lowlands and foothills on the southern Pacific slope, extending locally up the lower slopes of the Talamanca and coastal ranges to about 1,850 meters. It uses humid evergreen forest, forest edges, and nearby secondary woodland, usually moving through the upper canopy. Records are local and irregular, and birds may be absent from a site for long periods.
value.migrationStatus: Generally considered resident in Costa Rica and Panama, with no regular long-distance migration documented. Local movements may occur in response to food availability, and sightings can be irregular even within suitable Costa Rican habitat.
value.breeding: Available observations indicate breeding in the early part of the year, with reproduction reported in Costa Rica during March. The nest is a shallow, lightly built cup made from tendrils, fibrous strands, and similar plant material, placed on a horizontal branch, often in a partly isolated tree within forest. A recorded nest was about 9 meters above the ground and contained two buff-colored eggs marked with brown. Detailed information on courtship, incubation, and parental care remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: The Turquoise Cotinga is primarily a canopy fruit-eater. It takes small fruits and berries from trees and shrubs, swallowing many items whole and helping disperse seeds through its movements. It may also consume some insects and other small arthropods, particularly when feeding young or when fruit is less available. Birds usually forage alone or in loose groups and often remain unobtrusive among the upper branches.
value.behavior: This cotinga is usually quiet and spends much of its time high in the forest canopy. It is often solitary, although small, loose groups of up to several birds may form around food sources. Males can produce a soft wing sound during flight. Because it moves widely through treetops and may pause for long periods without calling, it is easily overlooked. Its irregular appearance at individual locations makes patient observation especially useful in Costa Rica.

conservation.populationTrend: Declining, mainly because the species has a restricted distribution and continues to lose suitable humid forest.
conservation.threats: The principal threat is the clearing and fragmentation of humid forest for agriculture, pasture, plantations, roads, and other development. Habitat in Panama has been heavily reduced, while remaining forests in Costa Rica are not all adequately protected. Loss of mature and connected canopy forest may also reduce access to fruiting trees and breeding habitat.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect remaining Pacific-slope forests and strengthen biological corridors between forest reserves, especially around the Osa Peninsula, Carara, and southern Costa Rican foothills. Support reforestation with native fruiting trees, avoid clearing mature forest, and encourage bird-friendly farming practices. Reporting sightings to established bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of this uncommon species and help guide conservation action.
